summary: After Judas leaves, Jesus gives His disciples a new commandment to love as He has loved, and warns Peter that he will deny Him three times.
key_insight: Before Jesus foretells Peter’s fall, He says, “But I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail; and when you have returned to Me, strengthen your brethren.” Jesus did not pray that Peter would never stumble. He prayed that his faith would survive the fall, and He gave him work to do afterward.
story: When Judas had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him.” He called the disciples “Little children” and told them He would be with them only a little while longer. Where He was going, they could not come. {Jn}

“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another; as I have loved you, that you also love one another. By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another.” {Jn}

Simon Peter asked, “Lord, where are You going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going you cannot follow Me now, but you shall follow Me afterward.” Peter said, “Lord, why can I not follow You now? I will lay down my life for Your sake.” {Jn}

Jesus said, “Simon, Simon! Indeed, Satan has asked for you, that he may sift you as wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail; and when you have returned to Me, strengthen your brethren.” Peter answered, “Lord, I am ready to go with You, both to prison and to death.” Jesus replied, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster shall not crow this day before you will deny three times that you know Me.” {Lk}

Then He reminded them of the time He sent them out without money bag, knapsack or sandals. Had they lacked anything? “Nothing,” they said. But now whoever had a money bag should take it, and whoever had no sword should sell his garment and buy one. The Scripture must be fulfilled in Him: “And He was numbered with the transgressors.” They said, “Lord, look, here are two swords.” He answered, “It is enough.” {Lk}

When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus said to them, “All of you will be made to stumble because of Me this night, for it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, And the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after I have been raised, I will go before you to Galilee.” {Mt}

Peter protested, “Even if all are made to stumble because of You, I will never be made to stumble.” {Mt} Jesus told him that this very night, before the rooster crowed twice, he would deny Him three times. But Peter spoke more vehemently, “If I have to die with You, I will not deny You!” And all the disciples said the same. {Mk}
differences: Luke and John place the warning to Peter in the upper room; Matthew and Mark place it after the hymn, as they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Mark alone says the rooster would crow twice; Matthew, Luke and John speak simply of the rooster crowing.
Only John records the new commandment; only Luke records Jesus’ prayer for Peter and the two swords; only Matthew and Mark quote “I will strike the Shepherd” and promise to go before them to Galilee.

Peter’s vow is worded differently in each: “I will never be made to stumble” (Matthew), “I am ready to go with You, both to prison and to death” (Luke), “I will lay down my life for Your sake” (John).

fit.question: Luke and John place Jesus’ warning to Peter in the upper room. Matthew and Mark place it after they sang a hymn and went out toward the Mount of Olives. Where was Peter warned?

points.label: Warned more than once
points.text: Peter did not take one warning quietly; Mark says he spoke “more vehemently” (14:31). It is natural that Jesus warned him at the table, and that when He spoke on the way of the scattered sheep, Peter renewed his boast and heard the warning again. McGarvey takes this view.

points.label: A loose “then”
points.text: Matthew and Mark join the warning to the walk with a simple “then.” They may have gathered the sayings about scattering and denial together without fixing exactly where each was spoken.

fit.note: Peter’s boast and Jesus’ warning are the same in every account. The Gospels differ only on where the exchange took place, and a repeated warning fits them all.
fit.short: Jesus likely warned Peter at the table (Luke, John) and again on the way to the Mount of Olives (Matthew, Mark).

scene.label: The hymn
scene.text: Later Jewish writings say the Passover meal closed with the second part of the Hallel, Psalms 115–118. If so, just before leaving for Gethsemane Jesus sang such words as “I will take up the cup of salvation” (Psalm 116:13) and “I shall not die, but live, And declare the works of the LORD” (Psalm 118:17).

scene.label: Sifted as wheat
scene.text: Grain was shaken hard in a sieve to separate the kernels from chaff and dirt. Satan’s request recalls Job 1–2, where Satan asks to test Job. In Luke’s Greek, the “you” Satan asked for is plural, all the disciples; the “you” Jesus prayed for is singular, Peter.

scene.label: The stricken Shepherd
scene.text: In Zechariah 13:7, the LORD calls for the sword to strike “the Man who is My Companion,” the Shepherd, so that the sheep scatter. Jesus reads His arrest and the disciples’ flight in that light, and adds a promise Zechariah does not: He will gather them again in Galilee.

scene.label: Two swords
scene.text: Jesus’ words warn that the days of welcome were over and hostility was coming. His reply, “It is enough,” probably closes the conversation rather than approving armed defense; hours later He stopped the use of a sword and healed the wounded man (Luke 22:49–51).

scene.label: A new commandment
scene.text: Love for one’s neighbor was already commanded in Leviticus 19:18. What is new is the measure: “as I have loved you.” John later writes that this command is both old and new (1 John 2:7–8).

witnesses.matthew: Sets the warning on the way to the Mount of Olives and anchors the disciples’ scattering in Zechariah’s prophecy of the stricken Shepherd. Even in the warning he records the promise, “after I have been raised, I will go before you to Galilee,” where the risen Jesus will meet the eleven (28:16).
witnesses.mark: Gives the most exact warning: the rooster would crow twice. Mark’s Gospel likely draws on Peter’s own preaching, and it keeps the sharpest details of Peter’s boast; the early church did not hide its leader’s fall.
witnesses.luke: Alone records Jesus’ prayer for Peter and the charge to “strengthen your brethren” after he returns. Luke also includes the two swords and the words of Isaiah 53, so the night of betrayal is framed by Scripture: Jesus will be “numbered with the transgressors.”
witnesses.john: Alone records the new commandment, given as soon as Judas leaves. John sets Peter’s promise to lay down his life beside Jesus’ answering question, and later the risen Jesus will ask Peter three times about his love (21:15–17).

seeing.reveals: Jesus loves His own with full knowledge of their weakness. He foresees Peter’s denial, prays for him before he falls, and already speaks of the restoration and the meeting in Galilee beyond it.
seeing.living: Peter trusted his own courage, and it failed before morning. Lean on Jesus’ prayer for you more than on your promises to Him. And the mark He gave His people is not bold vows but love for one another, measured by His love at the basin and the cross.
seeing.ponder: Where are you relying on your own promises to Jesus rather than on His prayer for you?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus’ disciples are known by His love, not by their bold promises.
preaching.watch_for: John sets two kinds of laying down a life side by side. Peter says, “I will lay down my life for Your sake” (13:37); Jesus, the Good Shepherd, is about to lay down His life for Peter (10:11; 15:13). The new commandment is measured by Jesus’ love, “as I have loved you,” not by Peter’s.

title: A New Commandment; Peter Warned
